hints: Count the carbons in butylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. All one step routes must start from a 4 carbon organic molecule so the skeleton does not change.
For the nucleophilic substitution route, think which C-X bond is easily broken by a nitrogen nucleophile to attach $\text{NH}_2$ directly.
For the other two routes, look for functional groups that already contain nitrogen bonded to the same 4 carbon chain.

Recall the two common nitrogen containing functional groups that give a primary amine on reduction, one with a $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond and one with a $\text{C}=\text{O}$ plus $\text{NH}_2$ group.
Match reagents to functional groups: excess ammonia under pressure is for substitution, while powerful reducing agents that supply hydrogen are for nitriles and amides.
Check the rules: three different functional groups and three different reagents, so you cannot use the same reducing agent twice if you can avoid it.
walkthrough:
Keep the 4 carbon skeleton in mind**
You are making $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. In one step you cannot build up the carbon chain easily, so start by picturing three different 4 carbon molecules that already have the butyl group, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$, attached to something that can become $\text{NH}_2$.

Route 1 from a halogenoalkane by substitution**
A $\text{C-Br}$ (or $\text{C-Cl}$, $\text{C-I}$) bond is polar and Br is a good leaving group. Ammonia acts as a nucleophile and replaces the halogen: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + 2\text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{NH}_4\text{Br}$$ Use excess $\text{NH}_3$ heated under pressure or in a sealed tube. Excess is important to minimise further substitution to secondary amines.

Route 2 from a nitrile by reduction**
Butanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, already has all four carbons plus nitrogen. Reduction adds hydrogen across the triple bond: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$$ Suitable reagents are $\text{H}_2$ with Ni or Pt catalyst, or $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in dry ether, or Na + ethanol.

Route 3 from an amide by reduction**
Butanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$, also has the correct skeleton. Reduction removes the carbonyl oxygen: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2 + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Use $\text{LiAlH}_4$ or Na + ethanol, choosing a different reagent from the one you named for the nitrile to satisfy the question conditions.

Final answer: Starting compound 1: 1-bromobutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ (any 1-butyl halide); reagent: excess $\text{NH}_3$ heated under pressure / in sealed tube.
Starting compound 2: butanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$; reagent: $\text{H}_2$ + Ni or Pt catalyst / $\text{LiAlH}_4$ / Na + ethanol.
Starting compound 3: butanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$; reagent: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ / Na + ethanol (must be different from route 2).

hints: Write the order first by recalling everyday experience: aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia, while aromatic amines are much weaker.
Define what a base does in the Bronsted-Lowry sense, accepting $\text{H}^+$ using a lone pair on nitrogen.
Think how a butyl alkyl group pushes electron density toward nitrogen compared with H in ammonia.
Picture the lone pair on N in phenylamine overlapping with the pi system of the benzene ring and consider what that does to its availability.
walkthrough:
State the order clearly**
Think of strength as willingness to pick up a proton. The correct order is: $$\text{butylamine} > \text{ammonia} > \text{phenylamine}$$ So butylamine is most basic and phenylamine is least basic.

Link basicity to the lone pair**
All three act as bases by using the lone pair on nitrogen to form a dative bond to $\text{H}^+$: $$\text{R}_3\text{N} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{R}_3\text{NH}^+$$ Anything that makes that lone pair more electron rich and more available makes the base stronger. Anything that pulls it away makes the base weaker.

Explain why butylamine beats ammonia**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ the alkyl group is electron donating by the positive inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto nitrogen, increasing the negative character of the lone pair. The lone pair is therefore more readily donated to $\text{H}^+$ than the lone pair in $\text{NH}_3$, where H has no such donating effect.

Explain why phenylamine is weakest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ the p orbital containing the nitrogen lone pair overlaps with the delocalised pi system of the benzene ring. The lone pair is drawn into the ring and is delocalised. It is no longer fully localised on N and is much less available to accept $\text{H}^+$, so phenylamine is a far weaker base than ammonia.

Final answer: butylamine > ammonia > phenylamine (most basic to least basic).
Basicity depends on availability of the lone pair on N to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Butylamine is stronger than ammonia due to positive inductive (+I) electron donating effect of the $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$ alkyl group, which increases electron density on N.
Phenylamine is weaker than ammonia because the lone pair on N is delocalised into the benzene pi system, making it less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.
